h1: Beer with Mangalorean ghee roast and coastal Karnataka food
title: Beer with Mangalorean Ghee Roast | Craft Beer School
desc: Which beers suit Mangalorean ghee roast, kori rotti, fish gassi, pork bafat and neer dosa, plus how to handle ghee, tamarind and chilli.
teaser: Ghee roast is red, rich and tangy. Pick the wrong beer and it tastes of nothing but chilli.
standfirst: Mangalore and coastal Karnataka cook with ghee, coconut, tamarind and fiery Byadgi chillies. The food is rich and sharp at once. Here is how we would pair beer with it.
sections:
Mangalorean ghee roast is chicken, prawns or mushroom cooked in a thick red masala of roasted Byadgi chillies, tamarind, garlic and spices, finished with plenty of ghee. Byadgi chillies are prized for their deep red colour and moderate heat, so the dish looks hotter than it often is.

That gives you three things to handle: fat from the ghee, sourness from the tamarind and a steady chilli warmth. Carbonation handles the fat. Malt sweetness softens the heat. Low bitterness stops the chilli from turning harsh. A beer that does all three is the target.
Chicken ghee roast suits a malty lager

For chicken ghee roast our pick is a Vienna lager or a Märzen, around 5 to 6% ABV and 18 to 25 IBU. The toasted malt picks up the roasted chilli paste. Its gentle sweetness rounds off the tamarind, while lager carbonation clears the ghee between bites.

A hefeweizen is the softer alternative if your ghee roast is on the hotter side. Its banana and clove notes are an unusual but friendly match for the spice blend. Avoid a big West Coast IPA here: 60 IBU of bitterness plus chilli and tamarind makes for a hard, metallic finish.
Kori rotti, neer dosa and the coconut curries

Kori rotti is a Tulu Nadu favourite: a thin chicken curry rich with coconut milk, poured over crisp, dry rice wafers. Fish gassi is in the same coconut family, sour with tamarind. Neer dosa, the thin lacy rice crepe, sits beside many of these curries.

Coconut milk is fatty and slightly sweet. A Belgian witbier is a natural partner, its orange peel and coriander lifting the coconut. A crisp Pilsner is the safer choice with fish gassi, where you want the beer to clean up rather than add flavour. Our guide to beer with South Indian food covers more coconut based dishes.
Pork bafat and sukka want darker beers

Mangalorean Catholic pork bafat is cooked with a dark, roasted spice powder and vinegar. It is tangy, rich and deeply spiced. Chicken or mutton sukka, a dry dish with roasted coconut, is earthy and nutty.

Both can take a darker beer. A brown ale or a dunkel brings nutty, bready malt that meets roasted coconut head on. With bafat, a porter at 4.5 to 5.5% ABV works well: roast against roasted spice, while the vinegar cuts through the beer's body. Keep stouts on the dry side. A sweet stout tastes cloying next to pork fat.

Coastal Karnataka loves its fish fry: kane (ladyfish), anjal (kingfish) and bangude (mackerel), coated in red masala and rice flour, shallow fried until crisp. Fried food is the easy win for beer.

Pilsner, Kölsch or a light lager all work, with carbonation doing the job of a squeeze of lemon. If you want more flavour, a saison brings pepper and citrus notes that suit the masala. Serve these beers properly cold, 4 to 6 °C, because a coastal afternoon in Mangaluru is warm and beer warms fast in the glass.
Neer dosa and the vegetarian thali

Coastal Karnataka has a strong vegetarian tradition too, especially in Udupi cooking. A meal might bring rasam, saaru, coconut based palyas, a tangy gojju and pickle, with rice and neer dosa. The flavours are bright, sour and lightly sweet, with heat from green and dry chillies rather than fat.

Without ghee or meat to carry, a big malty beer feels heavy. A Kölsch or a Helles keeps things light. If you want flavour, a Belgian witbier at 4.5 to 5% ABV is the best all rounder: the coriander and orange in the beer echo the curry leaves and tamarind in the food. A gose, slightly salty and tart, is another fun match with a sour gojju, though it is a matter of taste. The point is to keep bitterness low, under about 20 IBU, so the sour notes in the food stay pleasant rather than sharp.
Taste the heat, not just the beer

One thing to try with ghee roast is a side by side test. Pour a light lager and a malty Vienna lager. Take a bite and sip the light lager, then repeat with the Vienna. Most people find the lighter beer tastes thin and lets the chilli dominate, while the malty one makes the dish taste rounder. That is malt sweetness balancing heat. You can learn to predict it.

Matching beer to food this way is a sensory skill. It depends on noticing sweetness, bitterness and carbonation as separate things rather than as one blur. Our Indian food and beer pairing guide explains the principles in more depth.

Your first step: order chicken ghee roast with neer dosa and ask for one pale lager plus one amber or Vienna lager. Taste them in turn and note which one let you finish the plate.
faqs: What beer goes best with Mangalorean ghee roast?
A Vienna lager or Märzen. Toasty malt suits the roasted chilli paste, gentle sweetness balances tamarind and carbonation clears the ghee.
Is IPA a good match for ghee roast?
Usually not. High bitterness combined with chilli and tamarind gives a harsh finish. Pick a malty lager or a wheat beer instead.
A Belgian witbier works well with the coconut chicken curry. A crisp Pilsner is a safe choice for coconut fish curries.
